title: Kinetic Energy
summary: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion — every moving object carries it, from a rolling skateboard to a flying football. It grows with speed (doubling speed gives FOUR times the energy) and with mass. Explore energy = ½ × mass × speed² on a ramp and track how fast motion turns energy into speed.

plainLanguageExplanation: Kinetic energy is the energy a moving thing carries — the energy of motion itself. Anything with mass that moves has some: a rolling ball has a little, a speeding truck has a lot. The amount is given by KE = ½ × mass × speed², measured in joules. Two kinks in that formula are famous. First, speed is squared, meaning doubling the speed doesn't double the energy — it quadruples it (2² = 4). A car at 120 km/h has four times the crash energy of the same car at 60 km/h! Second, mass counts too, but only once. The model hands you a cart on a track with a speed slider: bump the speed and watch the energy bar balloon with the square, while the mass slider scales it more gently. This is the energy behind brakes, crashes, sports, and every bump — the reason faster things hurt far more than they seem.

whyItMatters: Kinetic energy is the hammer behind every crash, brake, and fast ball — that's why speed limits exist and why crumple zones must absorb energy safely. Athletes, engineers, and cyclists all reckon with it: wind turbines gather kinetic energy from air, roller coasters spend it, and drivers feel it in the braking distance table. Understanding KE explains why doubling a vehicle's speed quadruples the danger and why light things at speed still hit hard.
didYouKnow: A 100 kg cyclist pedaling at 40 km/h has roughly 6,200 J of kinetic energy. If a train at the same speed weighed 600,000 times more, its energy would be 600,000 times bigger — a clear reason trains need enormous stopping distances.
